THERMAL BUDGETING AND SAFE POWER DENSITY IN MICRO/NANOROBOTIC SYSTEMS AT THE LIMIT Transient Heat Transfer x Power-Pulse Dynamics x Sample Safety Feng Cheng-en (33) x STARLI Second Research Family | Flagship F04 | Research-design edition v1.0 (October 2026) DESCRIPTION The ability of a micro/nanorobot to move under optical, magnetic, acoustic, or electrical actuation does not establish that its surrounding sample remains within a safe thermal envelope. Local hot spots, transient source overshoot, buried interfacial temperature gradients, accumulated heating across repeated pulses, thermal cross-talk among adjacent agents, and delayed heat release after power cutoff can all undermine an otherwise impressive demonstration. This research monograph examines how these distinct physical mechanisms might be measured and bounded, and which observations would falsify a proposed safe-power claim. The book develops a prospective, nonclinical research architecture coupling transient heat transfer, power-pulse control, and independently evaluated material or specimen function. It begins with a declared whole-system energy boundary: source power, optical or field absorption, substrate conduction, fluid advection, contact resistance, fixture loss, cooling infrastructure, sensor burden, and physical shutdown. The central candidate field model is a transient advection-conduction energy balance, complemented by scoped relations for thermal diffusivity, Fourier/Peclet/Biot scaling, contact temperature jumps, pulse relaxation, radiometric and fluorescence observation, inverse heat-source reconstruction, covariance-aware uncertainty, and bounded control. An exposure index formed by integrating temperature exceedance is explicitly treated as a material-specific screening construct, not a universal injury law. The reference experiment is a controlled, sealed nonclinical microfluidic test bench using characterized surrogate heaters, inert thermal tracers, multiple phantom/substrate classes, and independent thermometry. Proposed qualification tests include blind pulse schedules, unknown flow and thermal-contact variations, one-agent versus ten-agent comparisons, probe-induced bias tests, physical-stop fault injection, post-cooling functional assays, and external reconstruction of a locked protocol. Success must be judged by the worst relevant temperature location, the quality and coverage of the uncertainty model, preservation of specimen function, and acceptance of a fully recovered task. Model accuracy cannot be repaired retrospectively by changing coefficients after the blind result is known. THERMAL BUDGETING AND SAFE POWER DENSITY IN MICRO/NANOROBOTIC SYSTEMS AT THE LIMIT Transient Heat Transfer x Power-Pulse Dynamics x Sample Safety Feng Cheng-en (33) x STARLI Second Research Family | Flagship F04 | Research-design edition v1.0 (October 2026) DESCRIPTION The ability of a micro/nanorobot to move under optical, magnetic, acoustic, or electrical actuation does not establish that its surrounding sample remains within a safe thermal envelope. Local hot spots, transient source overshoot, buried interfacial temperature gradients, accumulated heating across repeated pulses, thermal cross-talk among adjacent agents, and delayed heat release after power cutoff can all undermine an otherwise impressive demonstration. This research monograph examines how these distinct physical mechanisms might be measured and bounded, and which observations would falsify a proposed safe-power claim. The book develops a prospective, nonclinical research architecture coupling transient heat transfer, power-pulse control, and independently evaluated material or specimen function. It begins with a declared whole-system energy boundary: source power, optical or field absorption, substrate conduction, fluid advection, contact resistance, fixture loss, cooling infrastructure, sensor burden, and physical shutdown. The central candidate field model is a transient advection-conduction energy balance, complemented by scoped relations for thermal diffusivity, Fourier/Peclet/Biot scaling, contact temperature jumps, pulse relaxation, radiometric and fluorescence observation, inverse heat-source reconstruction, covariance-aware uncertainty, and bounded control. An exposure index formed by integrating temperature exceedance is explicitly treated as a material-specific screening construct, not a universal injury law. The reference experiment is a controlled, sealed nonclinical microfluidic test bench using characterized surrogate heaters, inert thermal tracers, multiple phantom/substrate classes, and independent thermometry. Proposed qualification tests include blind pulse schedules, unknown flow and thermal-contact variations, one-agent versus ten-agent comparisons, probe-induced bias tests, physical-stop fault injection, post-cooling functional assays, and external reconstruction of a locked protocol. Success must be judged by the worst relevant temperature location, the quality and coverage of the uncertainty model, preservation of specimen function, and acceptance of a fully recovered task. Model accuracy cannot be repaired retrospectively by changing coefficients after the blind result is known.
